newsitem.title: HUNGARY: NATO CHIEF SAYS LEBED WILL NOT SLOW DOWN EXPANSION.
newsitem.headline: NATO CHIEF SAYS LEBED WILL NOT SLOW DOWN EXPANSION.

text.p: NATO's top military official said on Tuesday NATO will not slow down its integration process despite comments by Russia's outspoken security chief Alexander Lebed that NATO should not hurry its expansion.

"NATO will stick to its chartered course -- it's nothing new and nothing confrontational," said General Klaus Naumann, the chairman of NATO's military committee, who was on a trip to Budapest to discuss NATO cooperation with Hungary.
Naumann met Lebed on Monday in Brussels during the Russian national security adviser's visit to NATO headquarters, his first ever trip to a western country.
Following the meeting, Lebed voiced grudging acceptance of NATO's plans to enlarge eastwards to take in some of Moscow's former satellites in eastern and central Europe.
Lebed said he accepted NATO's right to expand if it wished but said the problem was one of timing. "The main thing is not to hurry, or you may trip up," Lebed said.
Naumann described his talks with Lebed as constructive.
"They were conducted in a very civilised and moderate tone," he said. But he reaffirmed the timetable set out by NATO's political leaders will not change.

"What NATO wants to do is to achieve in a converging process a partnership with Russia that takes Russia's security interests into account and at the same time continues the course whch NATO adopted in 1994 when the decision was taken that doors should be open to democratic nations," he said.
NATO intends next year to invite countries to open entry talks, with Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic as the most likely candidates.
Naumann said a third round of discussions with 10 countries interested in joining NATO will be completed by the end of October and the findings presented to th NATO Council.

Naumann said that while internal and external reform of NATO structires was a parallel process it would be advisable for internal reform to be complete in time for negotiations start with prospectiove new members.
"Decisions are needed on internal adaptation before so that new members know what club they are joining," he said.

Naumann said he would be preparing a report on the military alternatives regarding any possible extension of the mandate for IFOR, the NATO-led peace implementation force in Bosnia, which is due to run out on December 20.
"As the NATO Secretary General (Javier Solana) has said the NATO nations are aware that Bosnia cannot be left on its own next year," he said.

"The military authorities will be tasked to study alternatives for potential political decisions. This will be authorised by the NATO Council in due time and then we can come back to the political authorities with our ideas," Naumann said.
U.N. diplomats said last month that two meetings -- one in November and one in December -- were planned to work out the basis for a continuing international involvement in Bosnia.

The first, expected to be held November 14 in Paris, would involve the Group of Seven top industrial nations, Russia and an Islamic representative. The second would be held in London with exact dates and participation still to be decided.
